title: Unveiling and Characterising Ubiquitous Nitrogen Enhancement in $6 \leq z \leq 10$ Galaxies with JWST Spectroscopy
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a growing number of $z>6$ galaxies with enhanced N/O ratios that challenge standard chemical enrichment frameworks. We test whether this is exclusive to extreme systems or a generic feature of $6 \leq z \leq 10$ populations through a stacking analysis of 135 galaxies with JWST/NIRSpec $R\sim1000$ spectroscopy, probing the origin of N, C and O enrichment and its dependence on recent star formation. A full-sample composite reveals prominent C III], C IV, N IV] and He II emission, demonstrating a ubiquity of high-ionisation UV lines. Auroral [O III]$λ$4363 electron temperatures and multi-ionisation zone modelling yield direct-$T_e$ abundances with supersolar $\log(\mathrm{N/O}) = -0.57^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and subsolar $\log(\mathrm{C/O}) = -0.80^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$ at $12 + \log(\mathrm{O/H}) = 7.79^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$, in contrast with local samples and suggesting significant nitrogen enhancement within the first billion years. Stacking further by recent star formation activity over burst timescales of $Δt = 3$--$20$~Myr, we find that sources caught in a recent burst are less enriched in both N/O and metallicity than those in a relative lull, with the largest contrasts confined to the shortest timescales. C/O, however, remains largely invariant across all metrics. We interpret these observations as the result of delayed AGB enrichment across multiple burst episodes, together with dilution by pristine gas inflows. Cosmological simulations reproduce this trend with CCSNe and AGB yields alone, without the need for shorter-lived (super-)massive stars. Enhanced N/O therefore appears to be a generic feature of high-redshift systems, produced by standard enrichment processes rather than requiring new physical frameworks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a stacking analysis of 135 z=6-10 galaxies observed with JWST/NIRSpec R~1000 spectroscopy, revealing supersolar N/O ratios and subsolar C/O ratios as a generic feature of high-redshift systems. Using direct-Te electron temperature measurements and burst-timescale stacking, the authors show that enhanced nitrogen comes from delayed AGB enrichment across multiple burst episodes with dilution by pristine gas, reproduced by standard CCSNe and AGB yields without invoking exotic stellar populations.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered z>6 galaxies with unusually high N/O ratios that challenge standard chemical enrichment models. The authors seek to determine whether this nitrogen enhancement is exclusive to extreme outlier systems or a generic property of the broader high-redshift galaxy population, and to identify its physical origin without resorting to new physics.
AI.method: Stacking analysis of 135 galaxies with JWST/NIRSpec R~1000 spectroscopy at 6≤z≤10. The team constructs a full-sample composite spectrum detecting C III], C IV, N IV] and He II lines. Auroral [O III]λ4363 measurements provide direct electron temperatures and Te-based abundances. They additionally stack the sample by recent star formation activity over burst timescales of Δt=3-20 Myr and compare results against cosmological simulations using standard CCSNe and AGB nucleosynthetic yields.
AI.result: The composite spectrum yields supersolar log(N/O)=-0.57 and subsolar log(C/O)=-0.80 at 12+log(O/H)=7.79. Sources caught in recent bursts show lower N/O and metallicity than quiescent ones, with the effect strongest at shortest timescales, while C/O remains invariant. Cosmological simulations reproduce these trends using only CCSNe and AGB yields.
AI.conclusion: Enhanced N/O is a generic property of early-Universe galaxies, produced by delayed AGB enrichment across multiple star formation episodes combined with pristine gas dilution. Standard enrichment frameworks (CCSNe + AGB yields) suffice; no exotic stellar populations or new chemical enrichment physics are required to explain the observed nitrogen enhancement at z>6.

title: A cosmic collision in the making: JWST/NIRISS reveals a merging and maturing protocluster core at z~3 around a red quasar
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 18 pages, 10 figures, including a 5-page appendix with 3 figures
summary: We report the discovery of ``The Step'', a dense protocluster at z=3 revealed by JWST/NIRISS Wide-Field Slitless Spectroscopy (WFSS) of the field around the luminous quasar and starburst SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3. The protocluster contains at least 18 member galaxies and exhibits two substructures in the 3D position-velocity space - notably a distinctive step-like distribution, from which the nickname derives. We propose that the Step may be undergoing a merger of two haloes, which could also explain the large velocity span (700-850km/s) between galaxies along the densest line of sight. This sightline contains seven galaxies within 70 projected kpc from the quasar, consistent with a remarkably dense protocluster core. We derive a galaxy overdensity of a factor >100 in the core and >15 within 1 Mpc$^2$, making it one of the densest structures known at this redshift, and a very massive halo of $13.1 < log M_{\rm halo}/ M_\odot < 13.8$, which suggests the structure could potentially evolve into a massive, Coma-like cluster at z=0. Compared to the field, the star-forming galaxies in the Step show slightly elevated levels of star formation. Yet, we find two quiescent galaxies with strong D4000 breaks and no evidence for ongoing star formation. Compared to other z=3 protoclusters, the Step exhibits similar or slightly suppressed star-forming activity. We also identify two new AGN candidates and find tentative evidence for an enhanced AGN fraction (10-20%) compared to the field. The protocluster constitutes one of the emerging handful of maturing structures at 2 < z < 4 that host both star-forming and quenched galaxies. This redshift regime may thus be a key transitional epoch for cluster studies, where overdensities transition from being the most active sites of star formation in the early Universe towards shaping the massive passive ellipticals seen in the cores of today's clusters.

AI.tldr: Discovery of "The Step", a dense protocluster at z=3 around quasar SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3, revealed by JWST/NIRISS WFSS. It contains ≥18 member galaxies with a distinctive step-like 3D structure, suggesting a merging of two haloes. The core has a galaxy overdensity >100, a massive halo (log M_halo/M_sun = 13.1–13.8), elevated star formation, two quiescent galaxies, and two new AGN candidates. It may evolve into a Coma-like cluster.
AI.motivation: To study the transitional epoch at 2 < z < 4 where overdensities evolve from the most vigorous sites of star formation into the massive passive ellipticals found in today's cluster cores, using a newly discovered dense protocluster seen in quasar environment.
AI.method: JWST/NIRISS Wide-Field Slitless Spectroscopy (WFSS) of the field around the luminous quasar and starburst SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3, enabling 3D position-velocity mapping of member galaxies, overdensity measurements, halo mass estimation, star-forming vs. quiescent classification via D4000 breaks, and AGN identification.
AI.result: The protocluster contains ≥18 members with a step-like 3D velocity distribution consistent with a two-halo merger, spanning 700–850 km/s along the densest sightline with seven galaxies within 70 projected kpc of the quasar. Overdensity >100 in the core and >15 within 1 Mpc^2; halo mass 13.1 < log M_halo/M_sun < 13.8. Slightly elevated star formation vs. field, two quiescent galaxies with strong D4000 breaks, and tentative AGN fraction enhancement of 10–20%.
AI.conclusion: The Step is one of the densest known z=3 structures and among the emerging handful of maturing protoclusters hosting both star-forming and quenched galaxies. The 2 < z < 4 regime may represent a key transitional epoch for cluster assembly, bridging active star formation in early overdensities and the passive ellipticals in modern cluster cores.

title: Flat Galactic Rotation Curves Interpreted as Evidence for the Mach's Principle
comment: Submitted. Comments welcome to aescala@das.uchile.cl
summary:
We explore the possibility of a Machian interpretation for the phenomena associated with asymptotically flat rotation curves in disk galaxies, providing an alternative to both the Lambda-Cold Dark Matter ($Λ$CDM) paradigm and MOdified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We argue that the MOND acceleration scale $a_0$ is likely not a new fundamental constant, but rather a manifestation of the cosmological scales of the observable Universe ($a_0 \sim c^2/R_u \sim c^4/GM_u \sim c/t_u$). We rewrite the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation (BTFR) in a cosmological format, $\frac{M_{\rm bar}}{M_{u}} = \left( \frac{V}{c} \right)^4$, suggesting that the transition to the non-Newtonian regime occurs when local accelerations become small enough to feel the global cosmic boundary, and showing that any Machian interpretation must fulfill a relation of this form. Furthermore, this framework naturally predicts a cosmological evolution of the BTFR normalization as the mass in the observable Universe evolves. We test these predictions against recent high-redshift observations ($z \sim 2$ and $z \sim 5$), finding that the data
  favor a flat, baryon-only, $Λ$-dominated quasi-de Sitter universe ($Ω_m \approx 0.05$, $Ω_Λ\approx 0.95$) over standard MOND or $Λ$CDM parameters. These results suggest that flat galactic rotation curves may be interpreted as compelling evidence in favor of Mach's Principle, in at least some of its versions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Machian interpretation for flat galaxy rotation curves, suggesting the MOND acceleration scale a0 is not a fundamental constant but derives from cosmological scales. It rewrites the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation in cosmological form and tests it against high-redshift observations, finding the data favor a baryon-only, Λ-dominated quasi-de Sitter universe, supporting Mach's Principle.
AI.motivation: To provide an alternative explanation for asymptotically flat rotation curves in disk galaxies that avoids both the ΛCDM dark matter paradigm and MOND as a modified gravity theory, by exploring whether the phenomena can be understood through Mach's Principle where local dynamics are influenced by the global cosmic boundary.
AI.method: The authors argue a0 ~ c²/R_u ~ c⁴/GM_u ~ c/t_u, recast the BTFR as M_bar/M_u = (V/c)⁴, and test the predicted cosmological evolution of the BTFR normalization against high-redshift observations at z~2 and z~5.
AI.result: The observations favor a flat, baryon-only, Λ-dominated quasi-de Sitter universe (Ω_m ≈ 0.05, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.95) over standard MOND or ΛCDM parameters.
AI.conclusion: Flat galactic rotation curves may be interpreted as compelling evidence in favor of Mach's Principle, in at least some of its versions.

title: Discovery of four Narrow-line Type-1 Quasars at z = 2.54 -- 6.06 with Subaru 'Onohi'ula PFS-SSP
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, submitted to PASJ
summary: We report the discovery of four narrow-line type-1 quasars (NLQ1s) from the Subaru 'Onohi'ula Prime Focus Spectrograph Subaru Strategic Program (PFS-SSP). To extend a comprehensive understanding of this population to the distant universe, we searched for broad-line AGNs (quasars) whose rest-UV spectral shapes resemble those of local NLS1 galaxies, utilizing the Ly$α$ line profile. We identified four NLQ1s, including one candidate, at $z=2.54$ -- $6.06$. The obtained spectra show a prominent Ly$α$ emission line with a very low continuum level. The measured full width at half maximum (FWHM) of Ly$α$ ranges from $1410 \ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ to $1510 \ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ with a mean of $\sim 1430 \,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Although we used only line width information for the NLQ1 selection, the resulting equivalent widths (EW) of Ly$α$ are higher (the mean $\sim 190$\,Å\ in the rest frame) than the typical values of quasars. Two quasars have exceptionally large Ly$α$ luminosity, accounting for $\sim 3$ -- $4$\% of the bolometric luminosity. We measured black hole masses and Eddington ratios for three objects whose C\,\textsc{iv} line is available. The resulting black hole masses are $\sim 10^{6.9}$ -- $10^{7.7}\, M_{\odot}$ with high Eddington ratios ($> 0.1$), consistent with those of NLS1 galaxies reported in the low-$z$ universe. N\,\textsc{v} and C\,\textsc{iv} broad absorption lines are detected in one object. This quasar can be classified as a mini-BAL quasar, which further supports the idea that this NLQ1 is indeed a luminous version of an NLS1 galaxy.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of four narrow-line type-1 quasars (NLQ1s) at z=2.54-6.06 from the Subaru PFS-SSP program, identified by their Lyα line profiles resembling local NLS1 galaxies. These quasars show narrow Lyα FWHM (~1410-1510 km/s), high equivalent widths (~190 Å), and three objects with C IV measurements have black hole masses of ~10^6.9-10^7.7 M⊙ with high Eddington ratios, consistent with low-redshift NLS1s. One object exhibits mini-BAL features (N V and C IV), supporting the NLQ1s as luminous NLS1 analogues.
AI.motivation: To extend the understanding of narrow-line type-1 quasars (luminous analogues of local narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies) to the high-redshift universe, where they have been poorly studied.
AI.method: Searched for broad-line AGNs whose rest-UV spectra resemble local NLS1 galaxies, using Lyα line profile (specifically line width) as the selection criterion from the Subaru PFS-SSP survey data.
AI.result: Identified four NLQ1s (including one candidate) at z=2.54-6.06. Lyα FWHM ranges 1410-1510 km/s (mean ~1430 km/s). Lyα EWs are higher than typical quasars (mean ~190 Å rest frame). Two have exceptional Lyα luminosity (~3-4% of bolometric). Black hole masses ~10^6.9-10^7.7 M⊙ with Eddington ratios >0.1. One object shows N V and C IV BAL features (mini-BAL quasar).
AI.conclusion: The discovered NLQ1s share physical properties (black hole masses and Eddington ratios) with low-z NLS1 galaxies, supporting them as the luminous, high-redshift counterparts of NLS1s. The mini-BAL detection further reinforces this classification.

title: Radiative Transfer Modeling of Stripped-envelope Supernovae II: Neural Network Emulation of Light Curves
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures
summary: We present the first neural-network emulator of stripped-envelope supernova (SESN) lightcurves, trained on a grid of 4499 light curves simulated with the radiative transfer (RT) code sedona. Using this emulator, we show that m_ni, m_ejecta, the ejecta velocity profile, and the degree of Ni-56 mixing can all be inferred from multiband lightcurves. We find that the degeneracy between ejecta mass and ejecta velocity is substantially weaker with this emulator than in traditional semianalytical models. The emulator is able to independently constrain the influence of ejecta mass and of ejecta velocity on the resulting lightcurve, rather than making them degenerate by design as traditional semianalytical models do. We additionally show that this inference is significantly more accurate than that done by the classical Arnett model for both simulated ZTF-like and LSST-like lightcurves. Finally, we present lightcurves fits to three well-studied SESNe: SN~1994I, SN~2007gr, and iPTF13bvn, constraining their m_ni, m_ejecta, and Ni-56 mixing.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first neural-network emulator of stripped-envelope supernova (SESN) lightcurves, trained on 4,499 simulations from the sedona radiative transfer code. It demonstrates that nickel mass, ejecta mass, ejecta velocity, and Ni-56 mixing can be inferred from multiband lightcurves, with significantly weaker mass-velocity degeneracy than traditional semianalytical models and more accurate inference than the classical Arnett model.
AI.motivation: Traditional semianalytical models like the Arnett model force a degeneracy between ejecta mass and ejecta velocity by design, limiting the accuracy of physical parameter inference from supernova lightcurves. A more accurate forward-modeling approach using radiative transfer simulations is needed, but these are computationally expensive. A neural-network emulator trained on such simulations provides a fast and accurate alternative.
AI.method: A neural-network emulator is trained on a grid of 4,499 stripped-envelope supernova lightcurves generated with the sedona radiative transfer code. The emulator is then used to perform Bayesian inference on mock observations (ZTF-like and LSST-like) and on real data from three well-studied SESNe (SN 1994I, SN 2007gr, iPTF13bvn), inferring m_Ni, m_ejecta, ejecta velocity profile, and Ni-56 mixing.
AI.result: The emulator successfully infers all key physical parameters from multiband lightcurves. It substantially weakens the mass-velocity degeneracy compared to semianalytical models, provides significantly more accurate inference than the Arnett model for both simulated ZTF-like and LSST-like lightcurves, and produces constrained parameter estimates for SN 1994I, SN 2007gr, and iPTF13bvn.
AI.conclusion: Neural-network emulators trained on radiative transfer simulations offer a superior approach for inferring SESN ejecta properties from lightcurves, overcoming the inherent degeneracies of classical analytical models and providing accurate parameter constraints for both simulated and real supernova observations.

title: An X-ray Absorption-Line Survey of the Circumgalactic Medium of M31 with XMM-Newton
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ. 13 pages, 5 figures, and 3 tables
summary: X-ray absorption line spectroscopy provides a powerful method for probing the extended hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) of individual galaxies. In this study, we present the first survey of \osv and \oeit absorption lines toward the hot halo of M\,31, using $15$ and $18$ background active galactic nuclei, with impact parameters ranging from $R_{\rm imp}\sim300$--$730$~kpc and $\sim190$--$730$~kpc, respectively. We find a marginal excess absorption above the expected Milky Way (MW) foreground toward the innermost sightlines, consistent with an additional hot-CGM contribution associated with M\,31. Comparing sightlines inside and outside $R_{\rm imp}=300$--$350$~kpc, the excess corresponds to a mean equivalent width of $\sim4$--$9$~mÅ for the inner \osv sightlines at $R_{\rm imp}\sim310$~kpc and $\sim17$~mÅ for the inner \oeit sightlines at $R_{\rm imp}\sim200$~kpc, with a nominal combined significance level of $2.2$--$2.3\,σ$. The hot-CGM mass inferred from this excess is highly model dependent, especially on the assumed CGM boundary, and therefore does not yet provide a robust baryon census. Attributing the excess entirely to hot gas confined within approximately the virial radius of M\,31 would require a CGM mass exceeding the nominal ``missing'' baryon budget. The inferred mass decreases to a few $\times10^{11}~M_\odot$ when the assumed CGM boundary is extended to $400-500$~kpc. Deeper observations, both through longer exposures of existing sightlines and the inclusion of additional inner-halo targets, will be essential to robustly constrain the properties of the hot CGM of M\,31.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first survey of O VI and O VII absorption lines probing the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) of M31 using 15 and 18 background AGN sightlines at impact parameters of ~190-730 kpc. A marginal excess absorption (~4-9 mÅ for O VI, ~17 mÅ for O VII) is detected toward inner sightlines at 2.2-2.3σ significance, but the inferred hot-CGM mass is highly model-dependent and does not yet provide a robust baryon census. The authors conclude that deeper observations are needed.
AI.motivation: To probe the hot, extended circumgalactic medium of the Andromeda galaxy (M31) using X-ray absorption line spectroscopy, in order to constrain the baryon content and physical properties of its hot halo.
AI.method: X-ray absorption line spectroscopy of O VI and O VII toward background AGN sightlines. The survey uses 15 sightlines for O VI and 18 for O VII, covering impact parameters from ~190 to ~730 kpc. Excess absorption above the Milky Way foreground is measured by comparing inner (R_imp < 300-350 kpc) and outer sightlines.
AI.result: A marginal excess absorption is found toward the innermost sightlines, with mean equivalent widths of ~4-9 mÅ for O VI at ~310 kpc and ~17 mÅ for O VII at ~200 kpc, at 2.2-2.3σ combined significance. The inferred hot-CGM mass is highly model-dependent; if confined to the virial radius, it would exceed the nominal missing baryon budget, but decreases to a few ×10^11 M_sun when the CGM boundary is extended to 400-500 kpc.
AI.conclusion: The detection of an M31 hot-CGM contribution is only marginal and model-dependent. More sensitive observations—longer exposures of existing sightlines and additional inner-halo targets—are required to robustly constrain the properties of M31's hot CGM.

title: Explaining the X-ray Precursor, Ultra-long Prompt Emission, and Week-long Decay of GRB250702B with a Jetted Micro-TDE
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, submitted to ApJL
summary: The longest detected gamma-ray burst, GRB250702B, exhibited seven hours of prompt $γ$-ray emission, preceded by a soft X-ray precursor ($\sim1$ day earlier) and followed by a weeks-long fading X-ray tail. Lacking an established progenitor for all three phases, we propose that this ultra-long GRB (ULGRB) is powered by a jetted micro-tidal disruption event (micro-TDE), in which a spinning stellar-mass black hole (BH) disrupts a Sun-like star and launches a relativistic jet via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism. Micro-TDE debris disks have hours-to-days viscous timescales, naturally explaining ULGRB durations. Using 3D hydrodynamic AREPO simulations of a $1\,M_\odot$ star disrupted by a $10\,M_\odot$ BH, we show that within $\sim1$ day the debris forms a quasi-steady envelope with a low-density polar funnel ($ρ\propto r^{-2}$, half-opening angle $\approx15^\circ$). Applying an analytic jet-stability framework to these profiles, we find that the $r^{-2}$ funnel keeps the jet below the kink-instability threshold, enabling stable propagation and breakout for jet powers, $L_{\rm jet}\gtrsim10^{47}$ erg s$^{-1}$. We attribute the X-ray precursor to pre-disk stream-fed accretion; the prompt GRB to a tightly beamed jet ($θ_{\rm b}\lesssim1^\circ$, $L_{γ,\rm iso}\sim10^{51}$ erg s$^{-1}$) escaping the funnel, launched by a rapidly spinning BH ($a_\bullet\sim0.9$); and the weeks-long X-ray decline to disk-wind mass loss ($L_{\rm jet}\propto t^{-2}$) combined with jet widening ($θ_{\rm b}\propto t$, initially steepening the decay to $L_{\rm X,iso}\propto L_{\rm jet}/θ_{\rm b}^{2}\propto t^{-4}$). Our model reproduces the multi-phase evolution of GRB250702B and establishes jetted micro-TDEs as a physically motivated ULGRB engine.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that GRB250702B, an ultra-long gamma-ray burst with a 7-hour prompt phase, an X-ray precursor ~1 day earlier, and a weeks-long X-ray tail, is powered by a jetted micro-tidal disruption event (micro-TDE), where a stellar-mass black hole disrupts a Sun-like star and launches a relativistic jet. Using 3D hydrodynamic simulations and analytic jet-stability analysis, the authors show that the debris forms a low-density polar funnel enabling stable jet propagation, and their model reproduces all three emission phases.
AI.motivation: GRB250702B is the longest detected gamma-ray burst with a complex multi-phase emission history (soft X-ray precursor, 7-hour prompt gamma-ray emission, and weeks-long X-ray tail), but no established progenitor model can naturally explain all three phases. The authors seek a physically motivated engine to account for the ultra-long duration and multi-phase behavior.
AI.method: The authors use 3D hydrodynamic AREPO simulations of a 1 solar-mass star disrupted by a 10 solar-mass black hole to model the debris envelope structure, then apply an analytic jet-stability framework to evaluate kink-instability thresholds. They connect the resulting jet properties (power, beaming angle) to the observed multi-phase emission, attributing each phase to a distinct physical mechanism: precursor to stream-fed accretion, prompt GRB to jet breakout, and X-ray tail to disk-wind mass loss combined with jet widening.
AI.result: The simulations show that within ~1 day the debris forms a quasi-steady envelope with a low-density polar funnel (density proportional to r^-2, half-opening angle ~15 degrees). The funnel configuration keeps the jet below the kink-instability threshold for jet powers above ~10^47 erg/s, enabling stable breakout. The model reproduces the observed multi-phase evolution: a tightly beamed prompt jet (opening angle <1 degree, isotropic gamma luminosity ~10^51 erg/s) from a rapidly spinning black hole, and a weeks-long X-ray decline following a power-law decay consistent with disk-wind mass loss and jet widening.
AI.conclusion: Jetted micro-TDEs are established as a physically motivated engine for ultra-long gamma-ray bursts, with the model successfully reproducing the multi-phase evolution of GRB250702B across precursor, prompt, and afterglow-like X-ray phases.

title: Spiral Morphology and Radial Migration: Kinematically heating, cooling, and cold
comment: 10 figures, 2 tables
summary: Transient spiral arms are known to drive radial redistribution of stars and thus could play a central role in shaping disk galaxies, including modifying, over time, the age, chemical, and kinematic (chrono-chemo-dynamic) distributions in the Milky Way. However, the physical factors governing the efficiency of such processes remain poorly understood. This paper investigates how the morphology of spiral arms -- the number, pitch angle, lifetime, and radial dependence of the pattern speed -- influences orbital redistribution through 'cold torquing' at the corotation resonance(s). Analytic expressions are derived for the maximum radial excursion of stars trapped at corotation that explicitly account for spiral morphology, predicting that the efficiency of cold torquing for a density-wave like spiral is greater for more open spiral patterns. Tracer-particle simulations confirm the analytic prediction, in both two- and three-dimensional galactic potentials. In contrast, spirals that have a radially dependent pattern speed such that they corotate with the disk at all radii exhibit the opposite behavior, with cold torquing becoming more efficient as the spiral winds to smaller pitch angles over time. This study further finds that resonant interactions from the same transient spiral causing cold torquing naturally also produces both kinematic heating and cooling of orbits away from corotation. These results demonstrate that spiral morphology alone cannot predict the efficiency of cold torquing and suggest that the relationship between spiral pitch angle and radial redistribution provides a potential diagnostic for distinguishing between competing theories of spiral structure.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how spiral arm morphology (number, pitch angle, lifetime, and radial dependence of pattern speed) influences radial orbital redistribution via 'cold torquing' at corotation resonances in disk galaxies. Analytic expressions show that for density-wave-like spirals, more open patterns (larger pitch angles) yield more efficient cold torquing—confirmed by tracer-particle simulations in 2D and 3D. However, spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds that corotate with the disk at all radii show the opposite trend. The same resonant interactions also produce kinematic heating and cooling away from corotation, demonstrating that spiral morphology alone cannot predict torquing efficiency and offering a diagnostic for distinguishing spiral structure theories.
AI.motivation: Transient spiral arms are believed to drive radial redistribution of stars in disk galaxies, shaping their chrono-chemo-dynamic distributions over time (e.g., in the Milky Way). However, the physical factors governing the efficiency of this radial migration through cold torquing remain poorly understood. This paper aims to fill that gap by systematically relating spiral arm morphology to the efficiency of orbital redistribution.
AI.method: The authors derive analytic expressions for the maximum radial excursion of stars trapped at corotation resonance, explicitly incorporating spiral morphology parameters such as number of arms, pitch angle, lifetime, and pattern speed radial dependence. They validate these predictions using tracer-particle simulations in both two- and three-dimensional galactic potentials, testing two spiral scenarios: density-wave-like spirals with radially constant pattern speed, and spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds that corotate with the disk at all radii.
AI.result: Analytic predictions confirm that cold torquing efficiency for density-wave-like spirals increases with more open (larger pitch angle) spiral patterns, verified by simulations in 2D and 3D. Conversely, spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds exhibit the opposite behavior—cold torquing becomes more efficient as the spiral winds to smaller pitch angles over time. Additionally, the same transient spiral that causes cold torquing also produces both kinematic heating and cooling of orbits away from corotation.
AI.conclusion: Spiral morphology alone cannot uniquely predict the efficiency of cold torquing, as the relationship between pitch angle and radial redistribution depends on the underlying spiral structure mechanism. This pitch-angle dependence provides a potential observational diagnostic for distinguishing between competing theories of spiral structure in disk galaxies.

title: Decoding the jet of BL Lacertae using relativistic magneto-hydrodynamics
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, accepted by A&A
summary: Blazars are a highly variable subclass of active galactic nuclei, whose relativistic jet is pointed towards our line of sight at a small angle. Their variability is often characterised by multi-band flares. BL Lacertae (BL Lac), the namesake of a blazar subclass recently exhibited the highest recorded linearly polarised optical flare. We investigate the origin of this flare via very-long-baseline interferometry observations. Our analysis shows that the sweeping, helical motion of the BL Lac jet, which is known to exhibit kink-like instabilities, can explain the observed flux density spike and polarisation angle rotation, as also confirmed by our state-of-the-art relativistic magneto-hydrodynamic simulations. As a by-product of these simulations we find that baryon loading of the jet is required to optimally replicate the observed jet morphology.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the origin of a record-high linearly polarized optical flare in BL Lacertae using very-long-baseline interferometry. The study shows that the sweeping helical motion of the jet, driven by kink-like instabilities, explains the observed flux density spike and polarization angle rotation, confirmed by relativistic magneto-hydrodynamic simulations that also reveal the need for baryon loading to match observed jet morphology.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical mechanism behind BL Lacertae's highest recorded linearly polarized optical flare, which is a key phenomenon in blazar variability, and to determine the structural dynamics of its relativistic jet.
AI.method: Very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of the BL Lac jet, combined with state-of-the-art relativistic magneto-hydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations to model jet dynamics and reproduce the observed flare characteristics.
AI.result: The sweeping helical motion of the jet, consistent with kink-like instabilities, explains the observed flux density spike and polarization angle rotation. The RMHD simulations further indicate that baryon loading of the jet is required to optimally reproduce the observed jet morphology.
AI.conclusion: The extreme optical flare in BL Lac can be attributed to helical jet motion associated with kink instabilities, and the simulations suggest a baryon-loaded jet is necessary to accurately describe the observed structure.

title: From Cluster Core to Splashback: Linking Dynamical Structure to Multidimensional Galaxy Evolution in the Coma Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in the ApJ
summary: We investigate galaxy evolution across the full dynamical structure of the Coma cluster using the GalWCat19 spectroscopic cluster catalog combined with SDSS-based value-added galaxy properties. We measure a splashback radius of $R_{sp} = 2.94 \pm 0.16~h^{-1}\, Mpc$. Using specific star formation rate (sSFR), color offset from the red sequence ($Δ(g-r)_{RS}$), and bulge-to-total ratio ($B/T$) as independent diagnostics, we find a coherent environmental transition from quiescent, red, bulge-dominated galaxies in the cluster core to increasingly star-forming, blue, disk-dominated populations at larger radii. We further introduce a three-dimensional framework in the joint $(\log sSFR, Δ(g-r)_{RS}, B/T)$ space and develop a peak-based classification scheme that extends beyond traditional one-dimensional galaxy classifications. This framework identifies two dominant populations: red, quiescent, bulge-dominated galaxies, which account for $51\%$ of the joint-analysis sample, and blue, star-forming, disk-dominated galaxies, which account for $29\%$. The remaining $\sim20\%$ of galaxies occupy transitional or mixed states that connect these two principal populations. These results show that the splashback boundary is not only a dynamical boundary, but also a critical evolutionary transition zone. Overall, our findings suggest that galaxy evolution in Coma is not a purely binary transformation, but instead proceeds through continuous multidimensional pathways in which star formation quenching, color evolution, and morphological transformation occur on different timescales while remaining closely linked to the cluster dynamical structure.

title: 3D Binary Neutron Star Merger Ejecta Evolution up to Seconds Timescale: Dynamics, Element Distribution, and Light Curves
comment: 25 pages, 19 figures
summary:
We present long-term, three-dimensional simulations of ejecta from four binary neutron star mergers to second-long time-scales. Numerical-relativity data serve as boundary conditions for a general-relativistic hydrodynamics evolution incorporating an equation of state valid outside nuclear statistical equilibrium and an effective nuclear-heating prescription based on reaction-network calculations. We investigate the ejecta's dynamical and geometrical properties, the impact of nuclear heating, the formation and spatial distribution of elements, and compute multi-angle kilonova light curves. %
Nuclear heating significantly affects ejecta dynamics, delaying homologous expansion beyond second time-scales and reshapes the spatial distribution of heavy nuclei. This effect is largest for asymmetric binaries with long-lived remnants; extending the evolution from ${\sim}150$~ms to ${\sim}1$~s widens the angular polar region containing 90\% of the heavy-element mass (\eg, $Z=56$, $Z=79$) from $|θ|\lesssim15^{o}$ to $|θ|\lesssim30^{o}$. Our nucleosynthesis results confirm that the $^{56}$Ni$\rightarrow^{56}$Co$\rightarrow^{56}$Fe decay chain dominates the heating at $\sim$100 days, with cobalt decay producing gamma-ray lines at 846.77 and 1238.288~keV. %
Comparing kilonova ray-by-ray light curves obtained from multi-angle 3D profiles and averaged 2D profiles, we find the latter approach broadly robust, although 2D light curves should be treated as upper limits. Increasing dimensionality generally lowers the bolometric luminosity, with binary asymmetry strengthening the viewing-angle dependence. For observers aligned with a lanthanide curtain's densest region, 3D emission can match its 2D counterpart in brightness. We conclude that increased dimensionality alone is unlikely to reconcile current theoretical models with AT2017gfo observations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents long-term 3D simulations of ejecta from four binary neutron star mergers extending to second-long timescales, showing that nuclear heating significantly affects ejecta dynamics and heavy-nuclei spatial distribution (widening polar regions from ~15° to ~30°). Nucleosynthesis confirms the 56Ni→56Co→56Fe chain dominates heating at ~100 days with gamma-ray lines at 846.77 and 1238.288 keV. Comparing 3D and 2D kilonova light curves shows 2D is broadly robust but yields upper limits; increased dimensionality alone cannot reconcile models with AT2017gfo observations.
AI.motivation: To understand the long-term dynamical evolution and nucleosynthesis of binary neutron star merger ejecta beyond typical short simulation times, and to assess whether increased simulation dimensionality can resolve discrepancies between theoretical kilonova models and AT2017gfo observations.
AI.method: The authors use numerical-relativity data as boundary conditions for general-relativistic hydrodynamics simulations, incorporating an equation of state valid outside nuclear statistical equilibrium and an effective nuclear-heating prescription derived from reaction-network calculations. They simulate four merger systems from ~150 ms to ~1 s, analyzing ejecta properties, nucleosynthesis, and computing multi-angle kilonova light curves comparing 3D ray-by-ray vs. averaged 2D profiles.
AI.result: Nuclear heating delays homologous expansion beyond second-long timescales and reshapes heavy-element spatial distributions, with asymmetric binaries showing the largest effects (polar region widening from |θ|≤15° to |θ|≤30°). The 56Ni decay chain dominates at ~100 days with characteristic gamma-ray lines. 2D light curves are broadly robust but serve as upper limits; 3D and 2D results can agree for observers aligned with densest lanthanide curtain regions.
AI.conclusion: Increased simulation dimensionality alone is unlikely to reconcile current theoretical kilonova models with AT2017gfo observations, though binary asymmetry strengthens viewing-angle dependence of emission.

title: Does IRS13 require an intermediate-mass black hole?
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, to appear in Proceedings of IAU Symposium No. 405 "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time"
summary: We investigate whether the Galactic-centre association IRS13 requires an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) to remain bound. Using high-precision $N$-body calculations of IRS13-like systems orbiting the Milky Way supermassive black hole (SMBH), as well as simulations of more massive infalling clusters, we find that an IRS13-sized cluster dissolves on a very short timescale even when an IMBH of $4\times10^4\,M_\odot$ is present. The observed velocity dispersion can arise naturally from the tidal field of Sgr A* and the infall event itself; therefore, it need not imply a central IMBH. In the infalling-cluster runs, tidal stripping produces transient disks, spiral-like structures, and ring-like overdensities. These features suggest a broader interpretation: IRS13 is best viewed as a temporary phase-space overdensity, analogous in mechanism (though not in scale) to phase-wrapped shells and streams in disrupted galaxies.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the Galactic-centre stellar association IRS13 requires an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) to remain gravitationally bound. High-precision N-body simulations show that IRS13-sized clusters dissolve rapidly even with a 4×10^4 M☉ IMBH present, and that the observed velocity dispersion can be explained by the tidal field of Sgr A* and the infall event itself. IRS13 is best interpreted as a temporary phase-space overdensity, analogous to phase-wrapped shells in disrupted galaxies, rather than evidence for an IMBH.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that the Galactic-centre stellar association IRS13 hosts an intermediate-mass black hole by determining whether such an IMBH is dynamically required to keep the system bound, or whether alternative explanations (tidal effects and infall dynamics) can account for the observed properties.
AI.method: High-precision N-body simulations of IRS13-like systems orbiting the Milky Way's supermassive black hole (Sgr A*), including systems with and without an IMBH of 4×10^4 M☉, as well as simulations of more massive infalling clusters subjected to tidal stripping.
AI.result: An IRS13-sized cluster dissolves on a very short timescale even when an IMBH of 4×10^4 M☉ is present, ruling out the IMBH as a binding mechanism. The observed velocity dispersion arises naturally from the tidal field of Sgr A* and the infall event itself. Infalling-cluster simulations produce transient disks, spiral-like structures, and ring-like overdensities consistent with observed features.
AI.conclusion: IRS13 does not require an intermediate-mass black hole to remain bound; it is best understood as a temporary phase-space overdensity created by infall dynamics and the Galactic tidal field, analogous in mechanism (though different in scale) to phase-wrapped shells and streams in disrupted galaxies.

title: Astrophysical Constraints on Hadron--Quark Crossover in Hybrid Neutron Stars
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables
summary: We investigate astrophysical constraints on hybrid neutron-star equations of state constructed by combining an extended linear sigma model description of quark matter with several representative hadronic equations of state through a smooth hadron--quark crossover. Four different hadronic models are examined in order to explore the model dependence of the resulting hybrid equations of state. After imposing stability, causality, perturbative QCD matching, tidal deformability, and maximum-mass constraints, only the eLSM+GMSR(BSK16) construction remains fully consistent with current astrophysical observations. The surviving parameterizations are further constrained using Bayesian inference based on NICER mass--radius measurements and the GW170817 gravitational-wave event. The posterior distributions favor a broad hadron--quark crossover occurring at relatively high baryon densities, while the formation of extended pure quark cores is strongly disfavored. Instead, the current observations favor neutron stars containing an extended mixed hadron--quark transition region. We also investigate the implications of the inferred maximum-mass distribution for the secondary object of GW190814 and find that, within the present model and adopted observational constraints, its interpretation as a neutron star is unlikely.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates hybrid neutron-star equations of state combining an extended linear sigma model for quark matter with four hadronic equations of state via smooth hadron-quark crossover. After applying astrophysical constraints, only the eLSM+GMSR(BSK16) construction remains viable. Bayesian inference on NICER and GW170817 data favors broad crossovers at high densities, disfavors pure quark cores, and suggests extended mixed hadron-quark transition regions exist.
AI.motivation: To constrain the behavior of quark matter in neutron stars by exploring model-dependent hybrid equations of state, and to determine which hadron-quark crossover scenarios are consistent with current astrophysical observations.
AI.method: Hybrid equations of state are constructed by combining an extended linear sigma model (eLSM) description of quark matter with four hadronic models via a smooth crossover. Stability, causality, perturbative QCD matching, tidal deformability, and maximum-mass constraints are applied, followed by Bayesian inference using NICER mass-radius measurements and GW170817 gravitational-wave data.
AI.result: Only the eLSM+GMSR(BSK16) hybrid equation of state survives all prior constraints. Bayesian posteriors favor broad hadron-quark crossovers at high baryon densities, strongly disfavor pure quark cores, and prefer extended mixed transition regions. The secondary object of GW190814 is unlikely to be a neutron star within this framework.
AI.conclusion: Current astrophysical data favor hybrid neutron stars with extended mixed hadron-quark regions rather than pure quark cores, and the inferred maximum-mass distribution rules out the interpretation of GW190814's secondary object as a neutron star in this model.

title: The Extended Mapping Obscuration to Reionization with ALMA (Ex-MORA) Survey: A Molecular Gas Line Search
summary:
Current investigations of cold gas in the interstellar medium face selection biases, as optical/near-infrared surveys favor massive, low-obscuration galaxies and miss gas-rich passive or inefficient star-forming systems. Overcoming this requires large-volume line surveys selected by molecular gas rather than stellar luminosity. We present a molecular gas census across $0.5 < z < 5$ using ALMA Band 4 observations from the Extended Mapping of Obscuration to Reionization Survey (Ex-MORA), covering 577 arcmin$^2$. Combining an unbiased search for bright emitters with a targeted search using spectroscopic redshift priors, we detect 52 galaxies in CO or \ci transitions (two showing two lines). Physical properties were derived via \texttt{CIGALE} with non-parametric star-formation histories, and gas masses were estimated using metallicity-dependent conversion factors.
  The sample is dominated by main-sequence (MS) galaxies with high stellar masses (median $\log M_*/\text{M}_{\odot} = 10.83$) and large gas reservoirs ($>10^{10}\,\text{M}_{\odot}$). Gas fraction ($μ_{\text{gas}}$) increases with redshift for active populations, though high-redshift trends are influenced by a gas-rich protocluster at $z \approx 2.4$. Conversely, an overdensity at $z \approx 0.73$ mirrors the field population. Five Green Valley (GV) galaxies exhibit a $μ_{\text{gas}}$ peak at cosmic noon, suggesting stellar feedback may suppress star formation by heating gas rather than rapidly depleting it in at least some transitional systems. Resolved kinematics show a prevalence of rotating disks. These results demonstrate that wide-area line searches effectively recover massive gas reservoirs across diverse evolutionary stages

The sample is dominated by main-sequence galaxies with high stellar masses (median log M*/M⊙=10.83) and large gas reservoirs (>10^10 M⊙). Gas fraction increases with redshift for active populations, with a notable gas-rich protocluster at z≈2.4 and an overdensity at z≈0.73. Five Green Valley galaxies show a molecular gas fraction peak at cosmic noon, suggesting stellar feedback suppresses star formation by heating gas rather than rapidly depleting it. Resolved kinematics reveal a prevalence of rotating disks.

This work aims to overcome this bias by performing large-volume line surveys selected by molecular gas rather than stellar luminosity.
AI.method: The study uses ALMA Band 4 observations from the Extended Mapping of Obscuration to Reionization Survey (Ex-MORA) covering 577 arcmin². It combines an unbiased search for bright emitters with a targeted search using spectroscopic redshift priors. Detection covers CO or CI transitions (52 galaxies, two with two lines). Physical properties are derived via CIGALE with non-parametric star-formation histories, and gas masses are estimated using metallicity-dependent conversion factors.
AI.result: 52 galaxies detected across 0.5<z<5, dominated by main-sequence galaxies with median log M*/M⊙=10.83 and gas reservoirs >10^10 M⊙. Gas fraction increases with redshift for active populations, though high-redshift trends are influenced by a gas-rich protocluster at z≈2.4. An overdensity at z≈0.73 mirrors the field population. Five Green Valley galaxies show a μ_gas peak at cosmic noon. Resolved kinematics show a prevalence of rotating disks.
AI.conclusion: Wide-area molecular-gas-selected line surveys effectively recover massive gas reservoirs across diverse evolutionary stages, providing an unbiased view of cold gas in galaxies beyond selection biases inherent in stellar-luminosity-selected surveys.

title: An Optically Motivated Gamma-ray Study of Fermi-LAT Novae
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 1 table
summary: High-energy (GeV) gamma-ray emission from nova eruptions was a surprise detection by the Fermi-LAT in 2010. Since then, it has been suggested that the gamma-rays from these systems are generated in collisionless non-relativistic shocks. In this theory, the observed correlation between optical and gamma-ray nova lightcurves naturally arises if a portion of the optical luminosity is reprocessed shock power. In this work, we investigate this scenario by analyzing Fermi-LAT-detected novae in varied time bins and then correlating the bin size that maximizes the nova's significance (tgam) with the nova's optical eruption data. Furthermore, we investigate whether there is a common optical decay across the sources' measured tgam values in the population. We find that across our population, a nova's $t_3$ (the time it takes the nova V band brightness to decay 3 magnitudes) appears to be the favored analysis bin that optimizes the Fermi-LAT detection significance, although there is significant spread. Additionally, we report V679 Car, a source previously noted as a marginally detected gamma-ray nova, as a $>5 σ$ detection in this work. We perform cross-correlation analysis of gamma-ray and optical lightcurves.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the connection between gamma-ray and optical emission in Fermi-LAT-detected novae, testing the theory that gamma-rays originate from collisionless non-relativistic shocks. By analyzing nova lightcurves in varied time bins and correlating the optimal bin size with optical eruption properties, the authors find that t3 (the time for V-band brightness to decay 3 magnitudes) appears to be the favored analysis bin for optimizing Fermi-LAT detection significance. They also confirm V679 Car as a >5σ gamma-ray detection and perform cross-correlation analysis of gamma-ray and optical lightcurves.
AI.motivation: Since the Fermi-LAT surprise detection of GeV gamma-ray emission from novae in 2010, the theory has been that these gamma-rays are generated in collisionless non-relativistic shocks. A natural prediction of this theory is that a correlation between optical and gamma-ray nova lightcurves should exist, since part of the optical luminosity would be reprocessed shock power. This work aims to test this scenario by investigating how time binning of Fermi-LAT data correlates with optical eruption properties across a population of gamma-ray-detected novae.
AI.method: The authors analyze Fermi-LAT-detected novae using varied time bins, then correlate the bin size that maximizes each nova's detection significance (tgam) with the nova's optical eruption data. They examine whether there is a common optical decay across the sources' measured tgam values. They also conduct cross-correlation analysis between gamma-ray and optical lightcurves for the sources.
AI.result: The authors find that across the population, t3 (the time for the nova's V-band brightness to decay by 3 magnitudes) appears to be the favored analysis bin that optimizes Fermi-LAT detection significance, although there is significant scatter. Additionally, they report V679 Car as a confirmed >5σ gamma-ray nova detection (previously only marginally detected).
AI.conclusion: The correlation between the optimal gamma-ray analysis bin (tgam) and the optical decay timescale t3 supports the shock-powered emission scenario for gamma-ray novae, consistent with the theory that a portion of the optical luminosity is reprocessed shock power. The confirmation of V679 Car adds a new source to the population of firmly detected gamma-ray novae for further study.

title: Constructing X-ray Spectral Models of Galaxies: Varying Contributions from X-ray Binary Populations with Host Galaxy Properties
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal (ApJ). 19 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables
summary: Recent work has shown that the emission from X-ray binary (XRB) populations in galaxies varies with stellar mass ($M_\star$), star formation rate (SFR), and metallicity ($Z$). Such scaling relations are widely used to predict the XRB contributions to galaxy-integrated X-ray luminosities including studies focused on dwarf active galactic nuclei (AGN) and the X-ray radiation field during the epoch of heating in the early ($z \geq 8$) universe. However, as galaxies approach low SFR and low $Z$, the relatively shallow slope of the XRB luminosity function (XLF) can yield very large stochastic variations in the total X-ray luminosity expected from the XRB population, for fixed values of $M_\star$, SFR, and $Z$. We have created a procedure to statistically sample any XLF and model total X-ray spectra for XRB populations and their stochastic uncertainties. We demonstrate the accuracy of this procedure using data for galaxies ranging from high to low $M_\star$, SFR, and $Z$ and generating X-ray spectral models consistent with Chandra observations. For galaxies that lie on the galactic main-sequence, we can relate SFR and $Z$ to $M_\star$ using established $M_\star$-SFR and $M_\star$-$Z$ relations. Applying these relations, we construct main-sequence (MS) XRB spectral models, which provide typical XRB spectral shapes, normalizations, and uncertainties as a function of $M_\star$. The spectral model library associated with this work is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20126734.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a statistical procedure to sample X-ray binary (XRB) luminosity functions and generate total X-ray spectra for XRB populations with associated stochastic uncertainties. The method is validated against Chandra observations across a wide range of galaxy properties, and MS XRB spectral models are constructed as functions of stellar mass using M*-SFR and M*-Z relations, with the spectral model library publicly available.
AI.motivation: XRB emission in galaxies scales with stellar mass, SFR, and metallicity, and these scaling relations are used to predict XRB contributions to galaxy-integrated X-ray luminosities. However, at low SFR and low metallicity, the shallow slope of the XRB luminosity function causes large stochastic variations in total X-ray luminosity, which existing approaches do not adequately capture.
AI.method: The authors develop a statistical sampling procedure to draw XRB populations from any XLF and compute total X-ray spectral models along with stochastic uncertainties. The procedure is validated using galaxies spanning high to low M*, SFR, and Z, with models compared against Chandra observations. For main-sequence galaxies, SFR and Z are tied to M* via established scaling relations, enabling the construction of MS XRB spectral models as a function of M*.
AI.result: The procedure accurately reproduces X-ray spectral models consistent with Chandra observations across galaxies with diverse properties. Main-sequence XRB spectral models provide typical spectral shapes, normalizations, and uncertainties as functions of stellar mass, and the spectral model library is released at a public repository.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a robust framework for modeling XRB populations and their stochastic X-ray variability, which is important for predicting XRB contributions in dwarf AGN studies and early-universe (z >= 8) X-ray radiation field analyses where stochastic fluctuations can be significant.

title: JWST Spectroscopy of Type Ia Supernova 2025rbs from Maximum Light to the Nebular Phase
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: We present JWST observations of the Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) 2025rbs ($D=$14.5 Mpc) at +1, +23, and +84 days after B-band maximum, spanning peak light through a wavelength-dependent transition toward the nebular phase. Combined with ground-based optical and near-infrared (NIR) data, our panchromatic spectra (0.4-14 $μ$m) include the first maximum-light mid-infrared (MIR) spectrum and the earliest MIR spectroscopic sequence of an SN Ia to date. At peak light, the MIR spectrum exhibits a continuum with permitted and forbidden features, including Si II, Ni II, and early-emerging [Ni III-IV] and [Ar II-III]. By +23 days the MIR is dominated by forbidden lines with a weak continuum, and by +84 days it is fully nebular, whereas the optical/NIR spectra remain transitional. The nebular spectrum reveals strongly stratified ejecta, with stable Ni concentrated at the lowest velocities, radioactive Co at intermediate velocities but absent within ~2000 km s$^{-1}$, and Ar occupying an outer shell. We detect small-scale substructure in [Ca IV] 3.21 $μ$m with fractional amplitudes of a few percent and a characteristic velocity scale of ~800 km s$^{-1}$, which may reflect compositional structure, ionization variations, or both. Radiative-transfer calculations substantially underpredict these MIR Mg II features despite approximately reproducing the NIR Mg II 1.0927 $μ$m line, suggesting that the relative strengths of these transitions are sensitive to the treatment of Mg ionization and excitation. These observations demonstrate that MIR spectroscopy beginning near maximum light simultaneously probes the emerging inner ejecta and rapidly fading outer burning products, providing new constraints for explosion and radiative-transfer models.

AI.tldr: JWST observations of SN Ia 2025rbs at +1, +23, and +84 days after B-band maximum provide the first maximum-light MIR spectrum and earliest MIR spectroscopic sequence of a Type Ia supernova, revealing stratified ejecta structure, substructure in [Ca IV], and a discrepancy in Mg II modeling.
AI.motivation: To obtain the earliest MIR spectroscopic coverage of an SN Ia, beginning at maximum light, to probe the emerging inner ejecta and rapidly fading outer burning products simultaneously, providing new constraints for explosion and radiative-transfer models.
AI.method: JWST MIR spectroscopy of SN 2025rbs combined with ground-based optical and NIR data, spanning 0.4-14 micron, at three epochs (+1, +23, +84 days after B-band maximum), with comparison to radiative-transfer calculations.
AI.result: MIR spectra show a continuum with permitted/forbidden features at peak (Si II, Ni II, early [Ni III-IV], [Ar II-III]), transitioning to fully nebular by +84 days. Nebular spectra reveal strongly stratified ejecta (stable Ni at lowest velocities, radioactive Co at intermediate velocities but absent within ~2000 km/s, Ar in outer shell). Small-scale substructure detected in [Ca IV] with ~800 km/s velocity scale and few-percent amplitudes. Radiative-transfer models underpredict MIR Mg II features despite reproducing NIR Mg II 1.0927 micron line.
AI.conclusion: MIR spectroscopy beginning near maximum light simultaneously probes emerging inner ejecta and fading outer burning products, demonstrating its power to constrain SN Ia explosion models and highlight deficiencies in current Mg ionization/excitation treatment in radiative-transfer codes.

title: The Rotation Curve of the Milky Way: State of the Art, the Keplerian Decline Debate, and Implications for Dark Matter
comment: 40 pages, 12 figures
summary: For four decades, the roughly flat rotation curve (RC) of the Milky Way (MW) stood as local evidence for an extended dark matter (DM) halo. \textit{Gaia} DR3 has changed the picture: several analyses now find a velocity decline beyond R \approx 15\kpc, and the most radical interpretation \citep{jiao2023} claims a nearly Keplerian fall-off (\vc \propto R^{-1/2}) that excludes a flat RC at 3σand implies a total dynamical mass of only \sim 2 \times 10^{11}\Msun---three to five times below pre-\textit{Gaia} estimates. Taken at face value, this would make the MW exceptional among comparable spirals and challenge both \LambdaCDM and MOND. It would also alter predictions for direct-detection experiments, although the local DM density is not fixed by virial mass alone. The Keplerian claim rests on the delicate assumptions of axisymmetric Jeans modelling, while stellar streams, globular clusters, satellite kinematics, and the Local Group timing argument generally favour a substantially heavier halo, and cosmological simulations reveal potentially substantial biases in Jeans-inferred outer RCs. This review offers a self-contained, pedagogical account of the debate: we derive the full formalism from first principles---the Jeans equations, the asymmetric drift correction, the standard DM halo and baryonic mass models, the MOND flat-RC prediction, and the timing argument---present an illustrative phenomenological MCMC fit and a Gaussian Process reconstruction of the RC, and critically assess which features of the decline can be regarded as established and which remain open.

AI.tldr: A pedagogical review of the controversy over the Milky Way's outer rotation curve, which Gaia DR3 suggests declines beyond ~15 kpc (possibly nearly Keplerian), challenging both the standard dark matter halo picture and MOND, while other probes favor a heavier halo.
AI.motivation: Gaia DR3 data have led to claims of a declining (even nearly Keplerian) Milky Way rotation curve, implying a much lower total mass than previously thought. This contradicts both LambdaCDM and MOND expectations and other independent dynamical probes, motivating a careful, self-contained assessment of what is actually established.
AI.method: The review derives the full Jeans-equation formalism from first principles, including the asymmetric drift correction, standard dark matter halo and baryonic mass models, the MOND flat-rotation prediction, and the Local Group timing argument. It presents an illustrative phenomenological MCMC fit and a Gaussian Process reconstruction of the rotation curve.
AI.result: The analysis critically assesses which declining features of the outer rotation curve are robustly established and which remain uncertain, weighing Keplerian-decay claims against stellar streams, globular clusters, satellite kinematics, and timing-argument evidence for a heavier halo, plus simulations showing biases in Jeans-inferred outer rotation curves.
AI.conclusion: The nearly Keplerian decline claimed from Jeans modelling of Gaia data remains unestablished; multiple independent probes favor a substantially heavier Milky Way halo, and systematic biases in Jeans-based inferences cast doubt on the radical interpretation.

title: Two new highly scattered fast radio bursts: evidence for scatter broadening by the circumsource medium
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables; submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: We found two highly scattered Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) during commissioning of the Commensal Realtime ASKAP Fast Transient COherent (CRACO) backend. FRB 240210D and FRB 240312D have scattering times of $34\pm6$ and $300\pm48$ ms, respectively, when scaled to 1 GHz. FRB 240312D originates near a spiral arm of a face-on galaxy at a redshift of only 0.05. Scintillation from a Milky Way screen constrains the distance of the scattering screen to $\sim 10$ pc from the source. FRB 240312D is therefore the first highly scattered FRB where scattering screens in the host galaxy centre, a background galaxy, or intervening structures can all be excluded, leaving only the circumsource medium. Integral field spectroscopy of the host reveals a Milky Way-like galaxy with a star-formation region at the FRB position. We find refractive scattering in a pulsar wind nebula as the most likely scattering origin. However, the explanation is not completely satisfactory as it requires a fine-tuned orientation. Hence, additional theoretical studies under different FRB progenitor models are needed. From the two FRBs, we calculate a total rate of $R_\mathrm{tot}=210^{+460}_{-180}\,\mathrm{events}\,\mathrm{sky}^{-1}\mathrm{day}^{-1}$ with durations between 55.2 ms and 1 s and above a fluence of 9 Jy ms consistent with the rate of shorter FRBs. This elevated rate suggests that the strong scattering seen in other FRBs likewise does not arise from chance-aligned sightlines, but is instead causally linked to the FRB sources.

AI.tldr: Two highly scattered Fast Radio Bursts (FRB 240210D and FRB 240312D) were discovered during CRACO commissioning. FRB 240312D, at z=0.05 near a spiral arm of a face-on galaxy, is the first highly scattered FRB where all distant scattering screens are excluded, localizing the scattering to ~10 pc from the source within a pulsar wind nebula. The inferred FRB rate suggests strong scattering is intrinsic to FRB sources rather than arising from chance-aligned sightlines.
AI.motivation: To determine the origin of strong scattering in FRBs by finding cases where the scattering screen can be unambiguously localized, and to assess whether such scattering is causally linked to the FRB sources or merely a line-of-sight effect.
AI.method: Commissioning observation with the CRACO backend on ASKAP; scattering time analysis scaled to 1 GHz; Milky Way scintillation constraints to localize the scattering screen; integral field spectroscopy of the host galaxy; rate calculation from two detections.
AI.result: FRB 240312D's scattering screen is localized to ~10 pc from the source, excluding host galaxy center, background galaxy, and intervening structures. The host is a Milky Way-like galaxy with star formation at the FRB position. Refractive scattering in a pulsar wind nebula is the most likely origin, though it requires fine-tuned geometry. A total rate of 210+460-180 events/sky/day above 9 Jy ms was measured.
AI.conclusion: Strong scattering in FRBs is likely causally linked to the FRB sources themselves rather than chance-aligned intervening media. The circumsource medium—possibly a pulsar wind nebula—is the scattering origin, though more theoretical work under different progenitor models is needed to fully explain the fine-tuned orientation required.

title: Electron temperature and emission measure of HII regions in the central molecular zone (CMZ) from H40 αrecombination line and continuum emissions by ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey - ACES -
comment: 20 pages, 17 pages, 2 tables, accepted for PASJ 08.08.2026
summary: Star formation activity in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) directly manifests itself as radio continuum free-free emission (Bremsstrahlung) and radio recombination line emission from HII regions surrounding newly formed massive stars. We derive the overall distribution of the HII regions and their fundamental properties: electron temperature ($\Te$) and emission measure ($EM$), and hence electron density in the form of two dimensional distribution maps over the CMZ by analyzing the ACES (ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey) \h40 (99.02 GHz) recombination line and 99.6 GHz continuum emission data with synthesized beam widths of $2''.45$ (0.097 pc at 8.2 kpc) and $2''.14$, respectively. We apply the 'TeEM' method ($\Te$--$EM$ mapping), which creates $\Te$ and $EM$ maps from input 2D maps of the continuum and integrated line intensity. title: Electromagnetic responses driven by gravitational-wave memory in magnetar-flare outflows
comment: 13 pages 6 figures
summary: An asymmetric relativistic outflow from a magnetar giant flare produces a step-like gravitational-wave (GW) memory. The principal response occupies the 10 kHz--1 MHz frequency band; a substantial extension into the 1--3 MHz frequency band also appears when a submicrosecond asymmetric-energy component is present. The electromagnetic response can escape from the source region and potentially propagate in the interstellar medium.

title: Scaling Relations of Galactic Outflows Across Cosmic Time: New Insights from Cosmic Noon
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 3 + 2 tables, accepted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Galactic outflows play a significant role in regulating galaxy evolution. With the joint sample, we explore the redshift evolution of outflow scaling relations. On average, outflows at Cosmic Noon have higher maximum velocities than those at low$-z$ by up to a factor of 3 for a fixed $M_\ast$, SFR, or SFR surface density. They also have higher mass outflow rates for a fixed $M_\ast$. Despite faster and stronger outflows, there is no evolution in the mass loading factor for a fixed $M_\ast$. We also constrain the overall outflow occurrence rate in our galaxy sample to be at least 30$\%$ when taking galaxy orientation and outflow geometry into account. title: Transmutation Timescales for Dark Matter Induced Collapse of Compact Stars into Black Holes
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D
summary: Ultra-heavy asymmetric dark matter (DM) particles captured by compact stars can thermalize, self-gravitate, and collapse to form an endoparasitic black hole (EBH), whose subsequent growth may transmute the host star into a black hole. We derive an analytical expression for the transmutation timescale by solving the EBH growth equation, consistently accounting for Bondi accretion of stellar matter, Hawking evaporation, and sustained DM feeding of the EBH in a steady-state capture regime. We also incorporate quantum effects in baryonic accretion when the hydrodynamic description breaks down, providing a unified treatment of EBH growth across both particle and fluid regimes. Adopting a physically transparent collapse criterion for fermionic and bosonic asymmetric DM, we compute EBH transmutation timescales for representative MSPs and WDs in environments with different DM densities. Although the physical ingredients are broadly similar to previous studies, this work derives updated constraints through a closed-form analytical treatment of EBH growth and an adopted prescription for the EBH formation timescale, yielding a lower critical EBH mass for sustained growth and revised transmutation timescales. Requiring the transmutation time to exceed $\sim 1$ Gyr for MSPs and $\sim 10$ Gyr for WDs, we derive revised constraints on $σ_{\rm nχ}$ over $m_χ\sim 10^{6}$--$10^{14}$ GeV, and show that EBHs with initial masses as small as $\sim 4\times10^{4}$ kg can undergo sustained growth, extending the region of DM parameter space probed by compact stars.

title: Real-time observations of the transition to the quiescent state in an accreting magnetised neutron star: No propeller required?
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, A&A, in press
summary: The final stages of outbursts in transient X-ray pulsars (XRPs), which are characterised by a significant decline in the mass accretion rate, provide valuable insight into the physics of the accretion disc and its interaction with the strong magnetic field of the neutron star (NS). In particular, the `propeller effect', or centrifugal inhibition of accretion, has been proposed as a key mechanism governing both the onset luminosity and the timescale of the rapid transition to the quiescent state. In addition, it offers an independent method for estimating the magnetic field strength of the NS. On the other hand, the decrease in the mass accretion rate itself is driven by processes occurring in the accretion flow at larger distances from the NS. Recovering the information encoded in the light curve therefore requires sensitive high-cadence X-ray monitoring capable of capturing the rapid and often unpredictable transition from the accreting regime to the quiescent regime. In this study, we present the results of the first comprehensive monitoring campaign that tracks the entire transition to quiescence in the transient XRP 4U 0115+63 utilising observations by the NICER X-ray telescope. We show that the observed behaviour can be explained by the thermal-viscous disc instability model (DIM), with the emission observed immediately after an outburst possibly arising from the ongoing accretion from the recombined (`cold') disc and the subsequent quiescent emission being produced by the cooling NS. We further applied this model to a larger sample of XRPs encompassing a broad range of physical parameters. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the temporal behaviour of XRPs, including the quiescent state, can be consistently explained within the DIM framework without requiring the propeller effect as the primary mechanism governing the observed transition.

title: Estimating the local star formation rate density from ASKAP RACS
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, published in PASA
summary: Understanding the evolution of the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) is key to uncovering how the Universe arrived at its present state. (2022, MNRAS, 515, 4711) catalogue as either galaxies or quasars using RACS-mid and WISE photometry. The full sample, consisting of 389,392 sources, was partitioned into a 70%-15%-15% split for training, validating, and testing. The optimised model achieved a weighted F1 score of 0.93 and an accuracy of 0.94 on the test dataset, ultimately classifying 336,674 sources as galaxies and 52,718 sources as quasars. Using the resulting $z<0.1$ depth-matched galaxy sample and the photometric redshift predictions from Beck et al. title: Synchrotron-Regulated Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence: Emission, Polarization, and Faraday Rotation
comment: Submitted to AAS journal
summary: Relativistic magnetized plasmas in many high-energy astrophysical systems are both turbulent and strongly radiative, yet their nonlinear dynamics and radiative outcomes remain poorly understood. Here we present results from three-dimensional driven turbulence simulations in relativistic magnetohydrodynamics with synchrotron cooling. We compute Faraday rotation measures, synthetic synchrotron spectra and linear polarization maps from the simulated turbulence. The balance between energy injection from turbulent driving and synchrotron cooling keeps the plasma, on average, relativistically hot, thereby influencing the rotation measure. Synchrotron cooling triggers the thermal instability and drives the plasma into hot dilute and cold dense phases, which enhances the spatial and temporal variability of synchrotron emission, especially at high frequencies. These diagnostics show qualitative similarities to observations of fast radio bursts, pulsar wind nebulae, and blazars, suggesting that turbulence may play an important role in shaping emission and propagation effects around high-energy sources.

They find that turbulence heating balances synchrotron cooling, keeping the plasma relativistically hot, while cooling triggers thermal instability that creates hot dilute and cold dense phases, enhancing spatio-temporal variability of synchrotron emission. The results qualitatively match observations of fast radio bursts, pulsar wind nebulae, and blazars.

title: Mapping the Inner Milky Way with Infrared-Derived Distances to AGB Stars
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures and 5 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The structure and evolution of the Milky Way (MW) can be traced with distance estimates to the evolved stellar populations in the inner galactic region. We find good agreement with reported distances for Galactic Mira variables and independent period-luminosity relations. Utilizing the expanded distance set, we further investigate the spatial distribution of Mira variables in the Galactic bulge and disk. Longer-period Miras preferentially trace the bulge's barred morphology compared to their shorter-period counterparts that populate the disk. We also find roughly constant, but differing, relative scale heights for the bulge and disk, with the bulge vertical dispersion about 30% larger. These findings show that IR photometry-derived statistical distances can recover large-scale Galactic structures and establish long-period Mira variables as efficient tracers of stellar populations in heavily obscured regions of the MW.

title: Wind-confined jet collimation revealed by the acceleration-phase photosphere of GRB 220426A
comment: Submitted. 12 pages + appendices
summary: We analyze the prompt emission of the exceptionally bright GRB 220426A observed by Fermi/GBM, whose time-resolved spectra are among the narrowest measured in any GRB. Here we show that observations during the first $\sim 5$s are consistent with the signal being emitted while the jet was still in the initial radiation-dominated acceleration phase. The time-resolved spectra allow the effective launch radius, $r_0$, to be inferred with unusual precision. We find $r_0 \sim \mathrm{few} \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm}$, increasing linearly with time. These findings match the theoretical predictions of the recollimation shock, suggesting that this GRB shows the first clear evidence for the existence and evolution of a recollimation shock. Using this interpretation, the linear increase observed is sustained over a period longer than expected from a pure jet breakout. Therefore, the jet collimation must have persisted even after breakout. We suggest that the collimation was maintained by a finite, dense, wind-like circumburst medium, which would reproduce the observed behavior of the prompt emission. We conclude that late-stage progenitor mass-loss can shape the earliest prompt emission and that the photospheric emission provides a way to probe both the jet collimation and the innermost region of the circumburst medium (CBM) surrounding the progenitor, independently of the constraints from interacting supernovae.
